a Roman army unit of about six thousand soldiers
s.c: The expression ‘twelve legions of angels’ indicates a very large group of angels; accordingly, the meaning may be rendered as ‘many, many angels’ or ‘thousands of angels.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the name of a host of demons
to speak or talk, with apparent focus upon the content of what is said
s.g: to say; to talk; to tell; to speak

s.d: to speak of a person or object by means of a proper name
to use an attribution in speaking of a person
s.c: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in ⟦Matthew 1:23|Matthew 1:23⟧ the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

s.d: to mark the correspondence in the meaning of foreign expressions
s.c: The meaning of λέγω must often be expressed in rather specific ways, for example, ‘which says in our language’ or ‘what is the same as what we say in our language.’

s.d: to say something in order to explain more fully the implications or intent of what has been said

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to speak to oneself) to think about something without communicating the content to others
s.g: to think to oneself; to say to oneself (often used to introduce a direct quotation of one’s thoughts)

s.d: a relatively small part which continues to exist

s.d: to be a continuing obligation
s.g: still ought to; still need to

s.c: In rendering ⟦Acts 9:18|Acts 9:18⟧ it is possible to say ‘there fell from his eyes something which looked like a fish scale’ or ‘… a small flake of skin.’

s.g: leper; one having a dread skin disease

s.d: a copper (or bronze) coin worth 1/2 of a quadrans or 1/128 of a denarius
s.c: In practically all instances, references to ἀσσάριον (LN 6.77), κοδράντης (LN 6.78), or λεπτόν may be made in terms of ‘a very small coin’ or ‘a coin with very little value’ or ‘money that was not worth very much.’

a member of the tribe of Levi and having the responsibility to serve as an assistant to Jewish priests
s.c: In most languages Λευίτης has simply been transliterated, but in other languages it is rendered as ‘assistant priest,’ especially in those contexts in which religious activity is involved.

s.d: (derivative of Λευί ‘Levi,’ son of Jacob, {D:93.231}) pertaining to being a descendant of Levi
s.c: The phrase ‘through the Levitical priesthood’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘by those priests who were descended from Levi.’

s.d: to cause something to become white
s.c: This statement in ⟦Revelation 7:14|Revelation 7:14⟧ may raise numerous difficulties for receptors, since blood would not be regarded as an instrument for making anything white. It may be necessary, therefore, to introduce a marginal note explaining the figurative language and suggesting the rendering ‘to make them pure.’

s.d: pertaining to being white or very light in color; applies to (parts of) the human body, animals, plants, inanimate objects
s.c: The term λευκός also occurs in ⟦John 4:35|John 4:35⟧ in speaking of fields being ‘white for the harvest,’ but in a number of languages it would be quite impossible to use the same term for the ripe condition of a harvest as in the case of the color of wool or snow. Furthermore, there may be a serious difficulty in speaking of wool as being ‘white,’ since in many parts of the world, wool is not regarded as being particularly white.

s.d: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source

largest of the great cats, often about 2.8 m from nose to tip of tail, standing as high as 1 m at the shoulder; pale yellowish brown in color; adult males have a mane around the neck and shoulders that is darker than the rest of their fur; Panthera leo; unclean animal; associated with aggression and strength
s.c: In some languages it may be important to use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a very large cat-like animal,’ though it will be important to try to make some distinction between ‘lion’ and ‘leopard’ (LN 4.13). If necessary, some more extensive identification by description may be employed in a glossary.

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Not Remembering, Forgetting
s.d: to not recall information and thus to lose sight of its significance
s.g: to forget; to not remember; to lose sight of; to ignore
s.c: In a number of languages the fact of ‘forgetting’ or ‘not remembering’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to lose out of one’s heart,’ ‘to have one’s thoughts walk away,’ or ‘to have words disappear from one’s liver.’

s.d: to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver, but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver{N:001}
an instrument for pressing out the juice of grapes for the making of wine
s.c: Ancient wine presses consisted of large vats into which grapes were placed and then trampled on in order to extract the juice. Accordingly, a descriptive equivalent of wine press may be ‘a place where the juice of grapes was squeezed out’ or ‘… pressed out.’

s.d: speech which is complete and utter nonsense
(derivative of ληστεύω ‘to practice robbery, piracy,’ not occurring in the NT) one who robs by force and violence
a person who engages in insurrection
generalized, positive degree
the aromatic resin of certain trees, burned for its pleasing aroma
s.c: Translators may either borrow a term such as ‘frankincense’ or use a descriptive equivalent, for example, ‘a sweet-smelling incense’ or ‘a valuable, sweet incense.’

s.d: a bowl in which incense is burned
(a Latin name) a group of people, presumably Jews, who had been slaves but later obtained their freedom; their synagogue was also known by the same name

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: (derivative of {L:λίθος<SDBG:λίθος:000000>}[a] ‘stone,’ {D:2.23}) pertaining to being made of or consisting of stone
s.c: In speaking of objects ‘made of stone’ it may be necessary in some languages to indicate more precisely the manner in which such objects have been formed, for example, ‘hewn out of stone’ or ‘made from stone by chipping.’

s.d: to kill or attempt to kill by means of hurling stones, normally carried out by angry mobs

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: stone as a substance{N:001}

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: a piece of rock, whether shaped or natural
s.c: Some languages make an important distinction between ‘stone’ as a substance (as in ⟦Acts 17:29|Acts 17:29⟧) and ‘stones’ as individual pieces of rock (as in ⟦Matthew 4:3|Matthew 4:3⟧). The term λίθος in the NT may be employed in speaking of rather large stones, for example, the stone placed in front of the tomb of Jesus (⟦Matthew 27:60|Matthew 27:60⟧) and the stones of the foundation of the Temple buildings (⟦Matthew 24:2|Matthew 24:2⟧). In all such contexts, however, the reference is to stones which have been moved into position or which are capable of being moved, even though with some difficulty.|In some languages an important distinction is made between stones which are shaped for use in building and stones which occur in a natural form, for example, ‘field stones.’ In each instance the biblical context must be studied to determine what type of expression should be used.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: valuable stones and hard substances, especially gems and jewels
s.c: For another interpretation of τίμιος in ⟦1 Corinthians 3:12|1 Corinthians 3:12⟧, see LN 65.2.|Precious stones are often distinguished on the basis of cost, appearance, or function, for example, ‘stones that cost much’ or ‘stones that are beautiful’ or ‘stones that are worn for decoration.’|A number of precious and semiprecious stones (see LN 2.30-LN 2.43) are mentioned in one NT passage, namely, ⟦Revelation 21:19|Revelation 21:19⟧, and though there are certain differences of opinion among scholars as to the precise reference of certain of these terms, there is more or less general agreement as to the color of the stones in question.|In languages in which terms such as ‘jasper,’ ‘sapphire,’ ‘agate,’ etc. exist, one may simply borrow such terms and explain their color in a glossary or word list. For languages in which such terms are not known, translators normally borrow the names from a dominant language of the area and likewise provide an explanation of the color in a glossary. Some translators have attempted to introduce the corresponding color terms in the text of ⟦Revelation 21:19|Revelation 21:19⟧, but this often results in a rather extended and somewhat awkward set of descriptive expressions.

s.d: A large, heavy stone used to close the entrance to a cave or tomb cut out of the rock
block of stone, either fully square or not; found in nature or hewn from a quarry; used for building houses, walls, and other constructions
an area in Jerusalem, paved with flat blocks of stone and forming a kind of courtyard (not a thoroughfare)
s.c: In some languages one may describe ‘The Stone Pavement’ as ‘a court covered with large blocks of flat stone’ or ‘a stone-paved courtyard.’ See LN 93.437.

s.d: to crush by a destructive amount of vertical pressure

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a relatively small area of the sea which is well protected by land but deep enough for ships to enter and moor
s.c: λιμήν may be rendered in some languages by a descriptive phrase, ‘a place where ships are safe from the storm’ or ‘a place where ships are never damaged’ or ‘a place where ships may stay.’ In ⟦Acts 27:12|Acts 27:12⟧ it is difficult to know whether the reference of λιμήν is to the harbor as a convenient place for the ships to stay during the winter, or to the port (that is to say, the town at the harbor) as a convenient place for people to stay during the winter. Some languages make a clear distinction between the area where ships stay and where people may stay waiting to continue their voyage.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a relatively small body of water either natural or artificial, surrounded by land
s.c: The use of λίμνη to refer to the Lake of Galilee (also called the Lake of Gennesaret) normally poses no special difficulty, but in the expression ‘lake of fire’ (⟦Revelation 20:10|Revelation 20:10⟧) there are complications, as already noted in LN 1.22.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: (an idiom, literally: lake of fire (and sulfur), occurring in some slightly different forms six times in Revelation, three times with the addition of θεῖον ‘sulfur’) a place of eternal punishment and destruction{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate literally ‘lake of fire,’ since water and fire seem to be so contradictory that a lake of fire is not even imaginable. It may be possible in some instances to speak of ‘a place that looks like a lake that is on fire,’ but in other languages the closest equivalent may simply be ‘a great expanse of fire.’ In some parts of the world people are fully familiar with the type of boiling magma in the cone of volcanoes, and terms for such a place may be readily adapted in speaking of ‘a lake of fire,’ since volcanic activity would seem to be the basis for this particular biblical expression.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a widespread lack of food over a considerable period of time and resulting in hunger for many people{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages the only way of talking about a famine is to say ‘many people were very hungry for a long time’ or ‘many people had to go for days without anything to eat.’ It is important to distinguish clearly between a famine and voluntary abstinence from food for the sake of fasting. (See Domain 53H.)

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare {L:νηστεία<SDBG:νηστεία:000000>}[a] ‘fasting,’ {D:53.65})
s.g: to be quite hungry; considerable hunger; lack of food
s.c: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: linen cloth, normally in the form of a garment{N:001}
s.c: Linen garments may be described as ‘clothing made out of linen cloth.’ What is important in ⟦Revelation 15:6|Revelation 15:6⟧ is the quality of the garments, not so much the fact that they were made of linen

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a linen cord in a lamp that draws up the oil
s.c: A wick may often be referred to as ‘a small strip of cloth.’

pertaining to being splendid, with the implication of luxurious
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 18:14|Revelation 18:14⟧ λαμπρός (LN 79.20) and λιπαρός serve primarily to reinforce one another.

s.dp: Weight › Pound, Talent [Specific Units of Weight]
s.d: a Roman pound, weighing about twelve ounces or about 325 grams
s.c: In speaking of perfume in ⟦John 12:3|John 12:3⟧ it may be far better to indicate quantity rather than weight, and therefore one may translate ‘then Mary took a pint of perfume.’ In translating λίτρα in the NT, one need not identify the pound as being ‘a Roman pound.’ It is better to employ a common term for pound (normally weighing sixteen ounces) or to provide a rounded-off equivalent of the amount in metric units, for example, three hundred grams or one-half liter.

s.dp: Spacial Orientations › North, South, East, West
s.c: As in the case of the intermediate direction ‘northwest’ (LN 82.5), one may also express ‘southwest’ in some languages as ‘a little south of west’ or ‘toward the south, but actually somewhat west’ or ‘veering to the right of south.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Take, Obtain, Gain, Lose

s.c: In some instances it may be important to translate λογεία as ‘to receive gifts of money,’ but the focus is upon the activity of the person or persons engaged in obtaining the contributions. This may be expressed in some instances as ‘to go from one person to another to receive their contributions.’

s.c: ‘To keep a mental record of something’ may be rendered as ‘to add up in one’s mind’ or ‘to make a list in one’s heart.’

s.g: to put into one’s account; to charge one’s account; to regard as an account

s.c: Since in ⟦1 Peter 2:2|1 Peter 2:2⟧ the context is figurative, some translators have preferred to render λογικός as ‘spiritual,’ so as to make the reference not literal but figurative.

pertaining to attractive and convincing speech
s.c: It is also possible to understand λόγιος in ⟦Acts 18:24|Acts 18:24⟧ as meaning ‘learned’ (see LN 27.20).

s.c: It is also possible to understand λόγιος in ⟦Acts 18:24|Acts 18:24⟧ as meaning ‘eloquent’ (see LN 33.32).

s.d: to think about something in a detailed and logical manner
s.g: to think about; to reason about; to ponder; reasoning

s.d: fallacious and deceptive reasoning and, by implication, based on evil intentions
s.c: It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘false arguments,’ especially if the equivalent of ‘arguments’ is a verb meaning ‘to argue’ or ‘to discuss against someone.‘ One can, however, express the semantic content of ‘false arguments’ (as reflected in λογισμός) by translating as ‘what people say when they argue, but their words are not true’ or ‘they argue with words that are not true.’

s.d: to argue or quarrel about the meaning or use of words
s.g: to quarrel about words; arguing about words

s.d: arguing or quarreling about the meaning or use of words
s.g: quarreling about words; arguing about words

s.d: that which has been stated or said, with primary focus upon the content of the communication
s.c: Any difference of meaning between λόγος and ῥῆμα would be only a matter of stylistic usage.|In ⟦Matthew 21:24|Matthew 21:24⟧ λόγος may be rendered as ‘question’ in view of the preceding ἐρωτάω ‘to ask’ (LN 33.180).

s.d: the act of speaking
the content of what is preached about Christ or about the good news{N:001}

a title for Jesus in the Gospel of John as a reference to the content of God’s revelation and as a verbal echo of the use of the verbs meaning ‘to speak’ in Genesis 1 and in many utterances of the prophets
a record of assets and liabilities
s.c: The phrase εἰς λόγον in ⟦Philippians 4:17|Philippians 4:17⟧ is a technical expression referring to the settlement of an account and indicates that this is a credit to the account. Accordingly, one may properly translate λόγον as ‘the amount of an account.’

s.d: a reason, with the implication of some verbal formulation

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View

s.g: to consider; to regard; to hold a view; to be of the opinion

s.d: a long weapon with sharpened end used for piercing by thrusting or as a projectile by hurling
s.c: Perhaps in ⟦John 19:34|John 19:34⟧ ‘spear point’

s.g: to slander; to insult strongly; slander; insult

s.c: In ⟦Ephesians 5:26|Ephesians 5:26⟧ the phrase τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος has been generally interpreted as a reference to baptism, since the literal washing of an object by means of water would not be a means of ritual purification in the sense in which the church would be dedicated or consecrated to God. Similarly, in ⟦Titus 3:5|Titus 3:5⟧, λουτρόν has generally been regarded as referring to baptism.

s.dp: Activities Involving Liquids or Masses › Use of Liquids

pertaining to the language spoken in Lycaonia
s.g: in the Lycaonian language; in Lycaonian

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a projection on the south coast of Asia Minor

wild, four-footed, predatory canine; light-brown fur, similar to jackal, but much bigger; Canis lupus; regarded as ravenous and fierce; commonly prey on flocks; symbol of roaming, opportunistic, dangerous, fierce, and clever banditry
s.c: In areas of the world in which wolves are not known, some translators have rendered λύκος by the local equivalent of ‘leopard’ or ‘jaguar.’ This may be satisfactory for initial translations of the Scriptures, but such shifts in reference are normally rejected at a later stage by those readers who become more acquainted with the types animals which exist in other parts of the world. In most instances in which local terms for ‘wolf’ do not exist, translators have used descriptive phrases such as ‘wild dog’ or ‘fierce, wild dog,’ or they may have borrowed a term from a dominant language in the area and have added a qualifying phrase, for example, ‘a wild animal called wolf.’ One may, of course, simply use a more generic expression with some kind of qualifier. For example, in ⟦Acts 20:29|Acts 20:29⟧ it is possible to use ‘fierce, wild animals,’ for the meaning of the passage is primarily figurative, and a specific designation of wolf is not required.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:λύκος<SDBG:λύκος:000000>}[a] ‘wolf,’ {D:4.11}) a person who is particularly vicious and dangerous
s.g: vicious person; fierce wolf; fierce person
s.c: In situations where wolves are not known, it may be possible to translate ⟦Acts 20:29|Acts 20:29⟧ as ‘men like fierce animals will come among you.’ In some instances λύκος in ⟦Acts 20:29|Acts 20:29⟧ has been rendered as ‘fierce, wild dogs.’

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: to cause injury or harm by maltreatment
s.c: It is also possible that λυμαίνομαι in ⟦Acts 8:3|Acts 8:3⟧ may mean ‘to destroy’ (see LN 20.31).

s.d: to destroy or to cause the destruction of persons, objects, or institutions
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult to find a general term for ‘destruction.’ What has often happened is the extension of meaning from a more specific type of reference, for example, ‘to smash,’ to a more generic meaning of ‘to destroy,’ and whether one understands the specific or more generic meaning depends largely upon the context. Accordingly, in ⟦Acts 8:3|Acts 8:3⟧ one may find a figurative usage of a term meaning ‘to smash’ (though understood in a more generic sense), for example, ‘Saul then worked in order to smash the church.’|It is also possible that λυμαίνομαι in ⟦Acts 8:3|Acts 8:3⟧ may mean ‘to injure severely’ (see LN 20.24).

s.d: (derivative of {L:λύπη<SDBG:λύπη:000001>}[b] ‘state of sadness,’ {D:25.273}) to cause someone to be sad, sorrowful, or distressed
to be sad as the result of what has happened or what one has done
s.g: to be sad; to be distressed

s.d: a state of unhappiness marked by regret as a result of what has been done
a state of mental pain and anxiety

s.d: a tetrarch of Abilene

s.d: Claudius Lysias, a Roman officer in Jerusalem; see {D:93.214}
to dissolve the marriage bond
s.c: Expressions for divorce are often based on terms meaning literally ‘to send away,’ ‘to separate from,’ or ‘to leave one another.’ However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are employed, for example ‘to send him off with his clothes,’ ‘to untie the knot between them,’ or ‘to throw away her hearthstones.’|Some persons have attempted to make an important distinction between ἀφίημι in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:11|1 Corinthians 7:11⟧ and χωρίζω in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:15|1 Corinthians 7:15⟧ on the assumption that ἀφίημι implies legal divorce, while χωρίζω only relates to separation. Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

s.d: to be of an advantage to someone
s.g: to be advantageous; to be better off; to be to someone’s advantage
s.c: In a number of languages the idea of ‘advantage’ implies some comparison, either a benefit which is greater than someone else has or a benefit which makes one’s later state better off than the previous state. For example, in the case of ⟦John 11:50|John 11:50⟧ one may translate ‘don’t you realize that if one man dies for the people, then you are much better off.’

s.d: a city in Lycaonia in Asia Minor
the means or instrument by which release or deliverance is made possible
s.c: ‘To liberate’ many may be expressed in many languages as ‘to cause people to go free’ or, in a more idiomatic manner, ‘to untie many’ or ‘to unchain many.’

s.d: to release or set free, with the implied analogy to the process of freeing a slave{N:001}
s.g: to set free; to liberate; to deliver; liberation; deliverance
s.c: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘being set free’ without specifying the particular manner or circumstances involved. In the case of ⟦Luke 24:21|Luke 24:21⟧, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘to liberate Israel’ as ‘to cause Israel to be free from foreign control’ or ‘… from the power of Rome.’ A similar type of translation may be required in ⟦Luke 2:38|Luke 2:38⟧, but in the case of ⟦Ephesians 1:7|Ephesians 1:7⟧ it may be necessary to specify ‘we are set free from sin’ or ‘we are set free from our bad desires.’

In the case of ⟦Luke 24:21|Luke 24:21⟧, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘to liberate Israel’ as ‘to cause Israel to be free from foreign control’ or ‘… from the power of Rome.’ A similar type of translation may be required in ⟦Luke 2:38|Luke 2:38⟧, but in the case of ⟦Ephesians 1:7|Ephesians 1:7⟧ it may be necessary to specify ‘we are set free from sin’ or ‘we are set free from our bad desires.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:λυτρόω<SDBG:λυτρόω:000000>} ‘to liberate,’ {D:37.128}) a person who liberates or releases others
s.c: The phrase ‘ruler and liberator’ may, of course, be expressed by a verbal form, for example, ‘as one who is to rule over you and to set you free.’

s.d: a stand designed to hold a single lamp or a series of lamps
s.c: One may translate ‘lampstand’ as ‘something on which a lamp could be placed’ or ‘a place for putting lamps.’

s.d: a light made by burning a wick saturated with oil contained in a relatively small vessel
s.c: In some languages the closest equivalent of λαμπάς and λύχνος is a kerosene lamp. What is to be avoided is a word which suggests a flashlight, which would of course be highly anachronistic.

s.d: to reverse the result of tying by untying
to release from control, to set free (highly generic meaning applicable to a wide variety of circumstances, including confinement, political domination, sin, sickness){N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages there are problems with a somewhat literal translation of λυθῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ δεσμοῦ τούτου in ⟦Luke 13:16|Luke 13:16⟧ since the expression is highly figurative. The reference, of course, is to the woman’s condition as a cripple. Furthermore, it may not make sense to speak of ‘Satan binding’ such a person, as in the first part of verse 16. In a number of languages, therefore, one may speak of ‘Satan causing the woman to be a cripple,’ and then in the latter part of verse 16, one may speak of ‘causing a person no longer to be a cripple.’

s.d: to destroy or reduce something to ruin by tearing down or breaking to pieces
s.g: to destroy; to tear down; to break to pieces
s.c: In some languages there may be an important distinction in terms meaning ‘to destroy,’ depending upon whether the destruction is purposeful or not. A still further distinction may arise on the basis of beneficial or non-beneficial results. In ⟦Ephesians 2:14|Ephesians 2:14⟧ the destruction is regarded as beneficial, while in ⟦Acts 27:41|Acts 27:41⟧ the opposite is the case.

s.d: to cause a gathering to be dismissed or dispersed
s.c: In some languages it may be more appropriate to render this expression in ⟦Acts 13:43|Acts 13:43⟧ as ‘when most of the people had left’ or ‘when the meeting was over.’

s.d: the failure to conform to a law or regulation, with a possible implication of regarding it as invalid
s.c: See also discussion at LN 36.29.

s.d: to exercise authority over something on the basis of its being legitimate
s.c: There are a number of different interpretations of the implication of this statement in ⟦Matthew 16:19|Matthew 16:19⟧, and translators should carefully review this passage in various commentaries.

s.d: to cause a state to cease{N:002}
s.g: to do away with; to remove; to eliminate

s.d: to cause to cease to exist
s.g: to cause to come to an end; to cause to become nothing; to put an end to
